full_base_rebuild_from_capri.status: every region rebuilt from CAPRI; base data now 98.5% of CAPRI UAA
full_base_rebuild_from_capri.note: The base data had been assembled by filling a TEMPLATE for all regions and overwriting it with CAPRI values only where a CAPRI code was found. Checking against CAPRI exposed three consequences: (a) 152 of the 154 checkable regions carried crops CAPRI does not record - about 3.5 Mha of template values (sugar beet 8.0, tobacco 1.0, fibre 1.0, set-aside 3.0 repeated region after region), including citrus in the Aosta Valley, grain maize in Finland and olives in northern Spain; (b) 100 of 248 regions had NO CAPRI source at all, because NUTS renamed or split them - all of France, Greece, Sweden, much of Italy and Poland, Ireland, Saxony, Croatia, Norway, and the countries CAPRI holds only nationally; (c) CAPRI's OFAR (fodder on arable land, 14.3 Mha EU-wide) and FALL (fallow, 5.5 Mha) had no counterpart in the model at all. REBUILT by tools/build/build_capri_base.py, one tool replacing the two single-case tools, because running two pipelines over the same files had already caused a real error. Regions map by: DIRECT (CAPRI's code is the region's own); RENAME, verified by matching CAPRI's own region names in its GAMS source against Eurostat's (FR240000 'CENTRE' -> FRB0 'Centre - Val de Loire', and so on for France, Greece, Sweden, Italy, Poland, Belgium, Romania, Bulgaria); MERGE (FI13 + FI1A -> FI1D); SPLIT by the children's own Eurostat cattle numbers (Saxony, Budapest/Pest, Warsaw area, Bolzano/Trento, Helsinki, Denmark, Lithuania, Slovenia, Croatia); IRELAND by the dual-coded year; NORWAY by pooling CAPRI's three redrawn regions, which cover the same territory as the model's four; ZERO where CAPRI records no agriculture. A STRUCTURAL DUPLICATE FOUND: Poland carried 21 regions where NUTS 2016 has 17 - the pre-2018 codes PL31, PL32, PL33, PL34 alongside their renamed equivalents PL81, PL82, PL72, PL84 - and both claimed the same CAPRI region, so Poland was counted TWICE (1.23x CAPRI). It was double-counted in the old data too, since the old codes held CAPRI values while the new ones held placeholders. Legacy rows emptied, as for Croatia's 2021 rows, Ceuta, Melilla and Brussels (1.6 Mha of phantom farmland between the three). RESULT: every country within 0.93-1.03 of CAPRI's own UAA, total 164,233 kha against 166,690 (98.5%). The missing 1.5% is exactly the CAPRI activities the model has no column for: paddy rice (427 kha), table olives (307), other marketable crops (1,156), nursery (181), flowers (118), other industrial (268). EU PRODUCTION IMPROVED MARKEDLY, and in composition rather than just totals: wheat area 19,854 -> 21,962 kha (real ~22,000), wheat production 113.6 -> 126.6 Mt (real ~130), grain maize area 11,737 -> 8,410 kha (real ~8,300) and production 91.7 -> 66.5 Mt (real ~65) - the old maize was inflated by 40%. Cereals total 288.8 Mt against the Commission Outlook's ~300. Validator 12/0/0, market prices still 12/12 against CAPRI PMRK, world balance 0.003%, 248/248 converge, base fidelity 0.59%.

nitrogen_balance_rebuilt.status: FIXED — two offsetting errors found once the areas were right
nitrogen_balance_rebuilt.note: Correcting the crop areas exposed that the nitrogen balance had TWO ERRORS THAT CANCELLED, which is why it had looked validated at 54 kg N/ha against a real EU ~46. ERROR 1 - MANURE COUNTED TWICE: the per-hectare nutrient coefficients were a TOTAL nitrogen concept, and the balance then added herd-derived manure on top. EU mineral nitrogen came to 16.5 Mt against a real ~10.8. ERROR 2 - FODDER UPTAKE DOUBLE-COUNTED: fodder crops are reported as FRESH matter (fodder maize 42.9 t/ha) but had no entry in the nitrogen-content table, so they fell to the 10 kg/t default and were credited with 429 kg N/ha against the ~180 a silage crop removes. Invisible while fodder was a placeholder; decisive once 14.3 Mha of real fodder was mapped in. A THIRD, SMALLER ONE: the fertiliser module's crop groups listed OFAR, TEXT and OIND - CAPRI's codes, not the model's columns - so the model's OFOD, COTT and OFIB matched nothing and received no mineral fertiliser. Same failure family as MAIZ/CORN. FIXED using CAPRI's own data: it reports mineral (NMIN) and manure (NMAN) nitrogen SEPARATELY per activity and region, and their EU totals - 9.47 and 5.89 Mt - match the real ~10.8 and ~7. Mineral nitrogen now comes from NMIN per region and crop (capri_data/2017/supply/nutrients_regional.csv), manure stays herd-derived, and fodder has fresh-matter nitrogen contents. A DEAD END WORTH RECORDING: NITF looked like the natural source for application rates but equals NRET, a nitrogen REQUIREMENT, not an application; summing area x NITF gives 29 Mt, far above any real figure. And an interim fix of mine - taking the maximum of coefficient and manure instead of the sum - produced a defensible EU average but put German regions at 14 kg N/ha, where Germany's surplus is among Europe's highest. Manure and mineral fertiliser do not substitute one for one. RESULT, every component now independently right: mineral 10.17 Mt (real ~10.8), manure 7.22 (real ~7), crop uptake 13.71 (real ~13-14), EU average surplus 44.5 kg N/ha and regional median 47.1 (real ~46), with a sensible regional pattern (Denmark 84, French arable core 80, Netherlands 65, Spain 40).

permanent_crop_f2f_gap.status: LARGELY CLOSED - all three crop groups now within 25% of published CAPRI
permanent_crop_f2f_gap.note: The Farm-to-Fork permanent-crop response is the model's largest unexplained discrepancy: -5.4% against CAPRI's published -12%. It is NOT an elasticity problem - permanent-crop elasticities match CAPRI's calibrated values to three decimals - so the four instruments were run SEPARATELY on the 25 most permanent-crop-intensive regions (6,952 kha of permanent crops). RESULT: pesticides -50% gives -1.66%, organic 25% -1.59%, the nutrient rule -0.79%, set-aside 10% -0.06%, all four together -3.57%; the instruments sum roughly linearly. NO SINGLE CHANNEL IS MISSING - every one is about a third as strong on permanent crops as CAPRI's. WHERE TO LOOK NEXT, by likely size: (a) the plant-protection cost share for permanents (ours comes from ES and IT PESTOTAL data - OLIV 24.3%, CITR 16.8% - while CAPRI's own documentation Table 1 implies a soft-wheat share about twice ours, so permanents may be understated too); (b) the pesticide yield-loss channel, which applies the same 10%-at-50% assumption to every crop, where fruit and vines depend on plant protection far more than cereals; (c) CAPRI's organic conversion, which may impose larger yield gaps on permanent crops than the flat 20% used here. Each is a measurable parameter, not a structural unknown.
permanent_crop_f2f_gap.fix: THE FAULT WAS THE COST CHANNELS, not the plant-protection share as suspected. CAPRI's pesticide scenario (JRC121368, stored in capri_data/sources/jrc121368/scenario_specification.json) has THREE channels: -50% plant-protection EXPENDITURE, +50% on OTHER INPUTS (mechanical weeding and alternative practices), and a 10% yield loss. This model applied the other-cost rise to the PLANT-PROTECTION share instead of the other-inputs share, so for wheat the saving (743 x 5.7% x 0.5 = 21 EUR/ha) and the rise (identical formula) CANCELLED EXACTLY and the entire cost channel was a no-op. Organic conversion had the same shape of error: a flat 15% premium on TOTAL cost, where CAPRI doubles other inputs and removes mineral fertiliser and plant protection entirely. WHY IT HIT PERMANENTS HARDEST: the other-inputs share, derived area-weighted from all 27 member-state capreg dumps (CAPRI's INPO over TOIN), is 47.8% for table grapes, 40.7% for wine, 30-34% for fruit and 29.7% for tomatoes, against 9.3% for wheat and 5.3% for durum. CAPRI's other-cost shock therefore bites about four times harder on permanents than on cereals - exactly the asymmetry the faulty implementation removed. The fertiliser share (CAPRI FERT over TOIN) runs the other way - wheat 41.6%, maize 44.3%, apples 1.2% - so organic conversion makes arable cropping CHEAPER while horticulture gets dearer, which a flat premium also hid. Both tables are now constants in supply_module (OTHER_COST_SHARE, FERT_COST_SHARE). RESULT on the headline comparison: oilseeds -13.1% -> -14.9% against CAPRI's -15%, a ratio of 1.00 (was 0.87); permanent crops -5.4% -> -7.0% against -12%, ratio 0.58 (was 0.45); cereals unchanged at -16.9% (1.13). All 8 anchors hold and 51/51 tests pass. STILL OPEN, and deliberately not tuned: permanents remain at 0.58 of CAPRI. The remaining candidate is the YIELD side - this model applies a flat 10% pesticide yield loss and a flat 20% organic yield gap to every crop, while CAPRI uses FADN-based gaps that are typically larger for fruit and vines. Without the FADN figures, adjusting those would be tuning parameters to close a gap rather than deriving them, which would make the agreement meaningless.
permanent_crop_f2f_gap.yield_side: THE YIELD SIDE IS NOW CAPRI'S OWN DATA, not a flat assumption. CAPRI does not hard-code its organic yield gaps: gams/pol_input/greendeal/organic_area.gms loads them from dat/pesticides/yield_effects_ppp.xlsx (sheet yld_gap), estimates made by JRC Seville from FADN data for the SUPREMA project, by PESETA macro-region and product group. The user supplied that file; it is stored at capri_data/2017/policy/organic_yield_gap.csv with CAPRI's own country-to-region and crop-to-group mappings (from gams/inputs/load_organic_yieldgap.gms) as constants in supply_module. The gaps are far larger and far more varied than the flat 20% they replace, and they differ by region as much as by crop: in Southern Europe, where most EU permanent crops are, fruits lose 22.5% and olives, vines and table grapes 11.6%, against cereals 16.1%; in Central Europe fruits lose 51.3%, cereals 42.9% and oilseeds 56.7%. A single EU-wide number could not represent that. RESULT on the headline comparison against published CAPRI (JRC121368): cereals -18.2% against -15% (1.22), oilseeds -18.8% against -15% (1.25), permanent crops -8.7% against -12% (0.72). Permanent crops improved from 0.45 through 0.58 to 0.72 as the cost channels and then the yield gaps were corrected, and ALL THREE GROUPS ARE NOW WITHIN 25% of CAPRI, with errors in both directions. A DELIBERATE NON-APPLICATION, recorded because it looked attractive: CAPRI multiplies these gaps by 0.45 in organic_area.gms, and the same factor appears in capreg/inputs/pest_cor.gms, because 55% of the measured organic gap is attributed to the loss of plant protection. It applies ONLY in CAPRI's endogenous-pesticide variant (pest_disagg==on), where that effect is solved through v_yldPestFac rather than assumed. The published runs compared against here use the exogenous 10% yield loss, which is what this model implements, so the full gaps are correct. Applying the factor was tested and moved permanent crops from 0.72 to 0.56 - away from the published result. The constant is kept, documented and unused, for the day the endogenous variant is implemented.

grass_yield_basis.status: resolved as far as the data allows
grass_yield_basis.note: The model's grass dry-matter yield was the last input with no verified basis against CAPRI - the ratio of model to CAPRI grass yield ran from 88 to 190 across regions, so no fixed transform existed. The reason is now clear: CAPRI's capreg carries NO physical grass yield. Its GRAS MPRI is a dummy 1000 EUR/t in every region (grass is not traded) and its GRAS YILD equals MREV exactly, so the 'yield' is a value construct, not a quantity. Checked across DE, FR, IE and NL. There is therefore nothing in CAPRI to validate the physical yield against. The model's value is externally plausible: median 4.64 t DM/ha with an interquartile range of 3.45-5.81, against a real EU permanent grassland yield of roughly 4-6 t DM/ha (higher in Atlantic regions, 2-3 in the dry Mediterranean). Its nitrogen uptake follows at about 70 kg N/ha, which is right for permanent grassland. Recorded as investigated rather than open: the absence of a CAPRI reference is a fact about CAPRI, not a gap in this model, and the value in use is defensible on its own terms.

table_olives_mapped.status: mapped; EU olive area now matches reality
table_olives_mapped.note: CAPRI separates olives for oil (OLIV) from table olives (TABO, 307 kha EU). The model has one olive column, and TABO was unmapped. Both are olive groves, so TABO now maps into OLIV: EU olive area 4,703 -> 5,010 kha, against a real EU olive area of about 5.0 Mha - a better match than either component alone. Validator 12/0/0 and all 8 anchors hold; olive base fidelity is 0.07%. STILL UNMAPPED, and left so deliberately: other marketable crops (1,154 kha), other industrial crops (268), nursery plants (181) and flowers (118) - about 1,721 kha, roughly 1% of EU agricultural area. These are distinct CAPRI activities with no natural home among this model's columns, and folding them into an existing crop would misrepresent them the way a flat premium misrepresented organic costs.

f2f_comparison_was_a_subset.note: Every Farm-to-Fork figure reported in this project was computed on the FIRST 30 REGIONS in index order, which are overwhelmingly German and Austrian. CAPRI's published figures are EU-wide. Run properly over all 248 regions the results are very different: cereals -6.54% against CAPRI's -15% (ratio 0.44, the subset said 1.22), oilseeds -10.92% against -15% (0.73, subset 1.25), permanent crops -4.74% against -12% (0.40, subset 0.72). THE CLAIM 'ALL THREE WITHIN 25%, ERRORS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS' WAS THEREFORE FALSE. The model under-responds to the Farm-to-Fork package across every crop group. WHY THE SUBSET FLATTERED IT: the organic yield gaps are FADN estimates by macro-region, and they are far larger in Central Europe (cereals 42.9%, fruits 51.3%) than in Southern Europe (16.1% and 22.5%). The 30 German and Austrian regions therefore see roughly triple the yield shock of the Spanish, Italian and Greek regions that hold most of the EU's permanent crops - and those regions were not in the sample at all. This is the same failure as the max_outer_iter=1 episode: a convenience setting chosen for speed became the basis of a published comparison. The comparison now lives in tools/run/run_policy_comparison.py, runs all 248 regions and to convergence by default, and warns if a subset is requested. PERFORMANCE, which is what made the subset tempting: the market module was doing 2.3 million scalar pandas .at[] reads and 1.7 million writes per run - 137 of every 140 seconds. Vectorising domestic_prices, supply_response and demand_response cut a 10-region converged run from 59 to 19 seconds with IDENTICAL results (all 8 anchors unchanged, market prices still 12/12 against CAPRI PMRK, world imbalance still 0.003%). A full EU comparison of two converged scenarios now takes 9 minutes, so there is no longer any reason to use a subset.

ppp_cost_shares_27_countries.note: Plant-protection cost shares were derived from Spain and Italy alone and were understated roughly threefold. They now come from ALL 27 member states: PESTOTAL (active ingredient, g/ha, from each res_17<CC> dump) times the national unit value UVAB.PLAP (EUR/kg, from coco), over TOIN, area-weighted. Wheat moves from 5.7 to 17.6 per cent, apples from 7.3 to 17.6; olives are stable at 24.9 against 24.3, which is why the two-country figure looked credible. THE EXTERNAL CHECK IS DECISIVE: applied to the base year, the old shares imply 3.57 bn EUR of EU plant-protection spending against a real market of 11-12 bn; the new ones imply 10.78 bn. CAPRI's own documentation had hinted at it - its Table 1 puts soft wheat plant protection near 11.5 per cent of input cost. AN INSTRUCTIVE SIDE EFFECT: correcting this alone made the Farm-to-Fork response SMALLER (cereals 0.44 -> 0.17 of CAPRI), because a larger plant-protection share means banning half of it saves more money, which offsets the yield loss. The parameter was still right; the scenario was missing its other half - see PESTICIDE_OTHER_COST_RISE.

pesticide_other_cost_rise_restored.note: PESTICIDE_OTHER_COST_RISE was set to 0.0, so CAPRI's +50 per cent other-cost shock was not applied at all. The reason was documented and sound at the time: 'other costs' is CAPRI's INPO category, the model had no equivalent, and applying the rise to the plant-protection share instead cancels the expenditure saving exactly - an artefact rather than a result, so it was zeroed and the omission stated. That reason stopped holding once OTHER_COST_SHARE was derived from INPO across all 27 dumps. The constant is restored to CAPRI's 0.50 and applied to the right base. Effect on net revenue at the 50 per cent target: French wheat -13.6 per cent, rape -31.6, Italian apples -14.9. WORTH NOTING: the zero was left behind by a correct decision whose precondition later changed. The comment explaining it was the thing that made the fix findable.

rail_overrode_policy_constraints.note: A post-solve 'safety rail' caps each activity at a multiple of its base level to stop pathological blowups under price shocks. Because it runs AFTER the optimisation, it could push the solution off constraints the QP had satisfied - and did. FR10 with a 10% set-aside requirement: floor 56.2 kha, QP solution 56.2, REPORTED 24.7, which is exactly 1.5x the base level of 16.5. Price shocks only arise from the second outer iteration onward, so SINGLE-ITERATION RUNS LOOKED CORRECT WHILE EVERY CONVERGED POLICY RUN QUIETLY RELAXED ITS LAND CONSTRAINTS. EU-wide, set-aside delivered 9.9 Mha against a 15.6 Mha requirement. Fixed: if clamping would violate a constraint, the constraint wins and the optimiser's solution stands. The rail still operates where nothing binds. A feasibility re-check was also added to the QP solver, which clipped negatives AFTER testing feasibility. NOTE FOR HONESTY: fixing this did NOT change the EU-wide Farm-to-Fork headline (0.39 / 0.95 / 0.57 before and after), because other instruments already push land use past the floor. The bug was real and worth fixing; it was not the cause of the under-response.

capri_own_price_elasticities.status: stored for all 26 CAPRI country groups
capri_own_price_elasticities.note: CAPRI's calibrated own-price supply elasticities (p_ElasSupp, 'CAL') for all 26 country groups (BL = Belgium and Luxembourg, IR = Ireland), 32 products, at capri_data/2017/supply/capri_own_price_elasticities.csv. User-supplied from their CAPRI installation. THE KEY FINDING is that the products split sharply. Across the 26 countries, permanent crops, horticulture and livestock vary by 1.0-1.6x (tomatoes and tobacco 1.0x, pork 1.1x, apples 1.4x), so they are effectively EU-wide constants - which is why setting them earlier from Spain and Italy alone worked, and why those crops now match the model. Annual crops vary by up to two orders of magnitude: barley 9.9x, maize 11.2x, potatoes 12.0x, rape 16.2x, oats 30x, pulses 42.7x, other cereals 56.2x, sunflower 141x. PER-COUNTRY TARGETS ARE THEREFORE MANDATORY for annuals; an EU-average would have been wrong for exactly the crops that drive the policy-response gap. WHEAT IS ABSENT from the parameter in all 26 files - no SWHE, DWHE or the market-model aggregate WHEA (arm_sets.gms maps (SWHE,DWHE).WHEA). It may be the numeraire whose elasticities follow from the system's adding-up conditions rather than being estimated. UNRESOLVED. A RELATED CORRECTION: an earlier comparison table in this project reported 'CAPRI 2.00' for soft wheat with a realized ratio of 0.46. That 2.00 was an ASSUMPTION of mine presented alongside genuine CAPRI values without being marked as one. Wheat is the largest EU crop at 22 Mha, so it carried the cereals conclusion. The conclusion survives on the measured crops (barley 0.51, maize 0.31, oats 0.30 of CAPRI), but the headline number was invented.

world_production_allocation_remeasured.note: This project has been reporting that 23.4% of world production is share-allocated rather than real. Remeasured against BOTH real sources - the 21-region FAO baseline AND the FAO_agg SUA extension, which the earlier figure evidently did not count together - the true number is 6.7%. 26 of 29 trade regions now carry real production data. The remainder: ROW 5.91% of world production, IRN 0.54%, SAU 0.25%. ROW is a residual aggregate by construction - 'rest of world' is not a country and cannot have a data source - so the only genuinely allocated countries are Iran and Saudi Arabia, together 0.8%, which CAPRI's own FAO aggregate does not separate from MIDEAST either. Both are small producers and large importers, so the allocated quantity is their least important property. FIXED WHILE MEASURING: the allocation multiplied each residual region's share by a seeded random factor of +/-8%. It was reproducible, but it was invented variation presented as data and served no modelling purpose. The allocation is now a deterministic production share, rescaled so the world total matches exactly as before. All 8 anchors unchanged, including price reproduction (12/12 against CAPRI PMRK) and world imbalance (0.003%). The lesson is the documentation one: a figure quoted repeatedly in summaries and the README was 3.5x too pessimistic because it was never remeasured after the data that fixed it was wired in.

standing_claims_audit.note: After two consecutive investigations found stale summary figures rather than live defects (world production allocated share, 23.4% against an actual 6.7%), the standing 'Validated' claims were re-checked rather than assumed. FALSE, now corrected: 'Supply - crops: realized own-price elasticities match CAPRI's PELA targets within ~10%'. Measured EU-wide against CAPRI's own calibrated values, permanent crops and horticulture do match (apples 0.89x, citrus 1.12x, vegetables 1.15x) but annuals do not: barley 0.51x, maize 0.31x, oats 0.30x, rape 0.14x. The original claim was measured against literature targets, not CAPRI's values, and reads as stronger than it was. WITHDRAWN rather than restated: 'N excretion matches CAPRI MANN within ~12%'. It predates the poultry unit conversion, and a direct re-measurement gives 1.38 - but CAPRI reports poultry in million head while other animals are in thousand, the exact unit trap that has produced two false readings in this project already, so the 1.38 is not trustworthy either. What IS verified is the absolute comparison against reality: manure N 7.49 Mt against a real EU ~7. The general lesson: a claim that is wrong is worse than an open question, because nobody re-checks it. Claims here should carry what they were measured against and when.

jrc121368_specification_verified.status: implementation confirmed against the published report
jrc121368_specification_verified.note: The published report (JRC121368, EUR 30317 EN, doi:10.2760/98160) was fetched directly - it is public, so this check needs no CAPRI installation - and its scenario specification (sections 4.3.1 and Tables 5, 9, 11) was compared item by item against this model. Every implemented channel matches: 50% cut in plant-protection EXPENDITURE (CAPRI models pesticides only as cost, not quantity); +50% in other costs for alternative practices such as mechanical weeding; a 10% yield loss applied to cereals, oilseeds, vegetables, other arable and permanent crops; and for organic conversion zero mineral fertiliser, zero plant protection, +100% other costs and FADN-based yield gaps. The landscape-features target is a set-aside requirement, as here. PROVENANCE OF THE 10% YIELD LOSS, previously unknown to this project: it comes from Sanchez et al. (2019). Of 20 pests reviewed, 18.6% of EU production was found potentially affected, and the report takes a worst case of 50% losses on that share. It is CAPRI's own reading of the literature, so it is not a parameter to tune. STILL NOT OBTAINED: section 5 holds the results by product, which is what would let this project compare crop by crop instead of against three EU aggregates (-15% cereals, -15% oilseeds, -12% permanent crops). The PDF extractor truncates before it. Other routes not yet tried: the report's annexes, the authors' EuroChoices article, and citing papers (Wesseler 2022; Beckman et al. 2022) which reproduce per-product figures. A MISMATCH TO CHECK BEFORE READING ANYTHING INTO THE REMAINING GAP: CAPRI's scenario is for 2030 and includes CAP reform variants, while this model's comparison runs from a 2017 base. That is the same class of apples-to-oranges error that has already produced three false conclusions here (the 30-region subset, the raw-column mismatch, and regional-versus-national elasticities).

yield_shocks_missing_from_output.status: FIXED — and it reverses the long-standing "cereals under-respond" finding
yield_shocks_missing_from_output.note: The pesticide yield loss and the organic yield gap were applied to NET REVENUE only, never to self.data.yields. They therefore steered what farmers grew but left gross_output computed on UNSHOCKED yields, so the yield effect was invisible in reported production. WHY IT MATTERED SO MUCH: CAPRI reports PRODUCTION, and its published cereal figure decomposes into an 11% yield fall and a 4% area fall (JRC121368, as reported in secondary coverage). This project had been comparing its AREA change against CAPRI's PRODUCTION change - the FIFTH apples-to-oranges comparison here, after the 30-region subset, the raw-column mismatch, regional-versus-national elasticities and the market-versus-PMP elasticity files. On the correct basis the finding INVERTS: EU cereal AREA falls 5.9% here against CAPRI's 4%, so the supply response was never too weak. The 'cereals at 0.39x of CAPRI' conclusion was a measurement error, not a model defect. FIXED by writing the shocked yields back, using the pattern apply_yield_price_response already used; _RESTORABLE already covers 'yields', so the mutation is undone per solve. A SECOND CORRECTION FOLLOWED. With yields reaching output, the run overshot: cereals -18.6% against CAPRI's -15%, oilseeds -27.7%, permanent crops -22.7%. CAPRI multiplies the organic yield gap by 0.45 when the pesticide yield effect is modelled separately, because 55% of the measured organic gap is attributed to losing plant protection (organic_area.gms; same factor in capreg/inputs/pest_cor.gms). An earlier version of this project TESTED that factor and rejected it - on AREA, the wrong metric. Applied, cereals land at -13.5% against -15% (0.90). REMAINING OVERSHOOT, with its cause identified: oilseeds -21.4% against -15% (1.43) and permanent crops -18.8% against -12% (1.57). CAPRI converts the DISTANCE from its projected 2030 organic area to the 25% target - roughly 13-15 percentage points, since the EU was near 9-10% - while this model converts a flat 25% of every region's area, nearly double the shock. Fixing that requires regional organic-area shares, which this project does not yet hold. All 8 anchors hold and the validator is 12/0/0 throughout.

organic_distance_to_target.status: FIXED — CAPRI converts the distance to the target, not the whole target
organic_distance_to_target.note: This model applied the 25% organic target as if every hectare converted. CAPRI does not: gams/pol_input/greendeal/load_organic_targets.gms sets p_organicAreaTarget('EU27yr19') = 0.25 - 0.10, a 15 percentage point shock, and breaks that down by member state from Eurostat organic areas. This model was applying nearly double CAPRI's shock, which is why oilseeds and permanent crops overshot. The converted share is now target minus ORGANIC_BASELINE_SHARE (0.10, CAPRI's own EU figure), applied to both the yield gap and the cost changes. CAPRI's per-member-state breakdown is computed in its R code from Eurostat data that this project does not hold, so the EU figure is applied uniformly and the simplification is recorded rather than hidden. RESULT on production, EU-wide, against CAPRI's published figures: cereals -13.8% against -15% (0.92), oilseeds -21.0% against -15% (1.40, was 1.43), permanent crops and vegetables -17.3% against -12% (1.44, was 1.57). All 8 anchors hold, validator 12/0/0. THE REMAINING GAP IS NOW ON THE AREA SIDE, and is better defined than before. Decomposing as CAPRI does: our cereal YIELD effect is about -11.6% against CAPRI's published -11%, so the yield channel now matches; our cereal AREA falls 2.5% against CAPRI's 4%. For oilseeds and permanent crops the area falls 10.0% and 4.9%, which - given a similar yield effect - implies CAPRI's areas fall only about 4.5% and 1%. So those two groups now CONTRACT TOO MUCH IN AREA, the opposite of the original diagnosis, and a narrower question than the one this project started with.
organic_distance_to_target.per_country_refinement: FOLLOW-UP, reported as a NEGATIVE RESULT. The residual overshoot on oilseeds (1.40) and permanent crops (1.45) was attributed to applying CAPRI's 15-point EU shock uniformly, where CAPRI breaks it down by member state. Per-country organic shares were taken from Eurostat org_cropar as published (Austria 25.3%, Estonia 22.3, Sweden 20.4, Czechia and Italy 15.2, Latvia 14.8, Finland 13.5, Slovenia 10.0, Netherlands 3.7, Poland 3.5, Romania 2.9, Bulgaria 2.3, Ireland 1.6, Malta 0.5) and wired in, with the EU figure as fallback for the countries Eurostat does not name individually. The mechanism works: Italy now converts 9.8 percentage points instead of 15, and Austria converts nothing at all, being past the 25% target already. IT CHANGED ALMOST NOTHING: cereals -13.82 -> -13.90%, oilseeds -20.95 -> -21.06%, permanent crops -17.32 -> -17.42%. So the uniform EU shock was NOT the cause of the overshoot. The refinement is kept because it is more faithful to CAPRI and rests on published data, not because it improved the fit. The residual overshoot therefore remains unexplained: oilseed and permanent-crop AREAS contract more than CAPRI's (ours -9.9% and -4.9%, CAPRI's implied roughly -4.5% and -1%), while the yield channel matches (our cereal yield effect -11.5% against CAPRI's published -11%). Coverage of the per-country table is partial by design: 14 of 27 countries, stated rather than filled in by guesswork.

jrc121368_results_decomposition.status: obtained — the comparison basis this project lacked
jrc121368_results_decomposition.note: The published report was read in full from the user-supplied PDF (the online fetch truncated before the results). It gives the AREA/YIELD decomposition that every comparison here needed and none had: CEREALS - area -4%, yields -11%, supply -15%. The area effect breaks down further: landscape elements alone cause -9%, partly offset because farmers EXPAND cereal area to compensate for the lower yields from organic and reduced-pesticide production, and the GNB target adds +0.6% through reduced herds and feed demand. VEGETABLES AND PERMANENT CROPS - area REMAINS STABLE at +0.1%, while supply falls 12%, 'explained by the drop in yields, mostly due to the organic yield gap'. LIVESTOCK - meat supply -14%, raw milk -10%, dominated by the GNB target. AGAINST THIS MODEL: cereals production -13.9% against -15% and cereal area -2.4% against -4%, both close. But our vegetables and permanent crops lose 4.9% of AREA where CAPRI loses none, which is the whole of the remaining discrepancy - its production falls 12% purely on yields, ours falls 17.4% on yields PLUS an area contraction that should not happen. The question is no longer 'why do permanent crops under-respond' (they over-respond) but 'why does permanent-crop area move at all'. CAPRI notes that land-use cross effects from the arable sector positively affect fruit and vegetable areas, which is the mechanism to look at. ALSO CONFIRMED: Annex Table A3.3 reproduces exactly the organic yield gaps already loaded here from yield_effects_ppp.xlsx, including the PESETA region membership (Central Europe North = BE, DE, LU, NL, PL; Central Europe South = AT, CZ, FR, HU, RO, SK; Northern Europe = DK, EE, FI, LT, LV, SE; Southern Europe = BG, CY, ES, GR, HR, IT, MT, PT, SI; Ireland separate), which matches the mapping wired into supply_module. One independent check of that data passed.

wine_price_silent_drop.status: FIXED — the cause of the permanent-crop area discrepancy
wine_price_silent_drop.note: The regional producer-price file carries CAPRI's activity codes for five crops this model names differently - TWIN for wine, TEXT for cotton and other fibre, OFAR for fodder on arable - so those columns were never read and the crops silently fell back to the EU-wide price. The same silent-drop family as MAIZ/CORN, the grassland codes, and the herd aliases. WINE WAS THE DAMAGING CASE. CAPRI prices it at a median of 1,362 EUR/t (2,453 in the French appellation regions, 403 in Spain's largest wine region); the fallback was 95.5. That left wine on a NEGATIVE gross margin in the biggest wine regions - Spain -712, Aquitaine -1,413 EUR/ha - where real EU wine margins are strongly positive at 2,000-6,000. An activity sitting at a negative margin responds erratically to any cost shock. HOW IT WAS FOUND, by decomposition rather than inference: the permanent-crop group was contracting 4.9% in area where CAPRI reports it STABLE at +0.1%. Splitting the group showed the model was right about almost all of it - olives, the largest permanent crop at 4.5 Mha, moved -0.10%, matching CAPRI exactly; citrus -2.6%, other fruit -3.1%, apples -3.7%. The contraction was wine (-11.3%) and vegetables (-9.3%), and vegetables are annual crops whose mobility is expected. The permanent-land constraint never binds (0 of 248 regions), which ruled out the land-structure explanation. AFTER THE FIX: wine -11.32% -> -2.58%, true permanent crops -4.11% -> -1.73% against CAPRI's +0.1% for the combined group, and the whole group (with vegetables) -4.94% -> -2.93%. Production -17.4% -> -16.7% against CAPRI's -12%. Base fidelity, all 8 anchors, validator 12/0/0 and 51/51 tests unchanged. WHAT REMAINS, and why this is as far as the evidence goes: CAPRI has a wine price for only 147 of 248 regions, so the rest still use the EU fallback - Sicily is one of them. And the residual overshoot on production is now dominated by VEGETABLES, which are annual crops; CAPRI reports them combined with permanent crops, so the +0.1% reference cannot be split to check them separately.

manifest_coverage_gap.note: Five inputs added during 2025-26 development were loaded and used but declared in NEITHER manifest: livestock_output_coef, livestock_revenue_coef, nutrients_regional, organic_yield_gap and capri_own_price_elasticities. INPUT_MANIFEST.json documents what each input is; MANIFEST.json carries the expected row and column counts that the validator checks. Missing from both, the files were invisible to the shape check - so a truncated or missing livestock coefficient file would have passed validation silently, which is precisely the failure mode the manifest exists to catch and which this project has hit repeatedly. Found while updating the README, because the README claimed 'every input the model consumes is declared' and that claim turned out to be false. FIXED: all five declared in both manifests with concept, unit, dimension, CAPRI symbol and shape; capri_own_price_elasticities also registered in loaders._FILE_CATEGORY so the validator can resolve it (it is reference data the model does not load, but it is shape-checked like any other file). VERIFIED BY BREAKING IT ON PURPOSE: truncating livestock_revenue_coef.csv to 99 rows now raises '99 rows (manifest 248)'; removing a file fails the presence check. The validator went from 25 to 30 files covered, and still reports 12 pass / 0 warn / 0 fail on the intact data.

schema_coverage_verified.status: claim verified and its scope corrected
schema_coverage_verified.note: The README's '99.4% of live cells are real CAPRI data' was checked rather than carried forward. Two problems. First, INPUT_SCHEMA.json declared 22 inputs while INPUT_MANIFEST.json declared 29, and a README edit had changed the count to 29 in a sentence that refers to the SCHEMA - so the stated number was wrong for the file it named. Second, and more substantive, the coverage figure was computed over those 22 inputs only: the five inputs added during development were outside it, so the headline percentage described a subset of the data layer rather than all of it. FIXED: all seven missing inputs declared in INPUT_SCHEMA.json with concept, unit, dimension, consuming modules, source and known gaps, so the schema and the manifest now agree at 29. Four apparent differences between the two files were only naming (schema 'trade_flows' against manifest 'trade_flows_2021.csv', and three similar). RECOMPUTED over the whole data layer: 123,159 real cells of 123,758 declared, 99.5%. The claim holds, and now means what it says. The README cites the tool that produces it (tools/check/verify_schema.py) so the next reader can re-run it rather than trust it.

rice_market_and_minor_activities.status: both closed — the model now reproduces CAPRI's agricultural area exactly
rice_market_and_minor_activities.note: TWO OPEN POINTS CLOSED TOGETHER, both bounded data work. RICE NOW HAS A MARKET. Paddy rice was an activity competing for land but not a market commodity, so it had no trade balance and no price feedback. The data was already held: CAPRI's own world price (capmod_world_prices_2017.csv, RICE 411.42 EUR/t) and FAO production, consumption and trade for 24 regions in the extended SUA file. PARI is now a market commodity with Armington parameters taken from other cereals, the nearest analogue. World rice balances exactly at 386,384 kt with the real producers - China 141,643, India 112,221, Indonesia 36,798, Vietnam 28,481. One alias was needed: FAO names paddy rice RICE while this model's activity is PARI, and reading the file without it would have dropped rice silently - the same failure as MAIZ/CORN and TWIN/WINE. THE FOUR REMAINING CAPRI ACTIVITIES ARE MAPPED: other marketable crops (1,154 kha), other industrial crops (268), nursery plants (181) and flowers (118). They had been left out deliberately rather than folded into crops they are not; CAPRI holds complete areas, yields, costs and prices for all four, so they are now activities in their own right. The model has 34 crop activities. RESULT: the model's agricultural area equals CAPRI's EXACTLY - 166,690 kha against 166,690, 100.0%, where it was 99.0%. Every CAPRI crop activity with a recorded area is mapped. The manifest earned its keep here: adding rice changed the row counts of world_prices.csv and armington_params.csv, and the shape check flagged both before anything else could absorb them silently. Shapes updated; validator 12/0/0, all 8 anchors hold, base fidelity 0.58%.

oilseed_permanent_overshoot.note: On CAPRI's own reporting basis (production, EU-wide, all 248 regions, converged): cereals -13.9% against CAPRI's -15% (0.93), oilseeds -21.1% against -15% (1.40), permanent crops and vegetables -16.7% against -12% (1.39). Cereals are close; the other two OVERSHOOT. WHAT IS NOT THE CAUSE, each ruled out by measurement rather than argument: the yield channel (our cereal yield effect is -11.5% against CAPRI's published -11%); land pinning (the arable shadow price is zero in all 248 regions); price feedback (without it cereals fall 7.0% instead of 5.9%); supply elasticities (they match CAPRI's own regional PELA values at 0.76-1.00, median 0.92); a uniform organic shock (applying CAPRI's 15 points per country from Eurostat organic shares moved the result by less than 0.2 percentage points); and catch crops (CAPRI models them as a winter-cover share, not a land competitor, and they REDUCE pest damage). WHERE THE RESIDUAL SITS. Decomposing the permanent-crop group: olives, the largest at 4.5 Mha, move -0.10% against CAPRI's 'stable'; citrus -2.6%, other fruit -3.1%, apples -3.7%. The contraction is concentrated in VEGETABLES at -9.3% - annual crops whose mobility is expected and which CAPRI reports MERGED with permanent crops. Its +0.1% reference for the combined group therefore cannot be split to check vegetables separately. WHY THIS IS AS FAR AS THE EVIDENCE GOES: closing it needs CAPRI's results per product, which the published report does not give at that resolution, and a CAPRI scenario run is not available. The remaining 1.39-1.40 is the limit of what this comparison can resolve, not a located defect. FOR THE USER: treat oilseed and permanent-crop scenario magnitudes as overstated; cereals, the yield channel and the area response are close to CAPRI.

livestock_intensity_margin.status: implemented and pinned by a test
livestock_intensity_margin.note: CAPRI carries every dairy herd twice, as a low- and a high-intensity variant (DCOL and DCOH). In the base year the split is MECHANICAL - the two levels are exactly half the herd in every region checked - and their yields average to the dairy yield this model already used (DE11: 6,287 and 10,481 kg/head, average 8,384). So representing them separately adds nothing to the base year. What they carry is a RESPONSE CHANNEL: a herd can move between intensities under policy, which is how CAPRI lets dairy extensify under a nutrient target instead of only shrinking. Without it the only livestock margin is the number of animals. IMPLEMENTED as an intensity margin rather than as extra activities, matching how crop nitrogen intensity is already handled: CAPRI's per-region DCOL and DCOH yields are extracted to livestock_intensity_bounds.csv (235 regions, EU median 5.39 and 8.99 t milk/head), and a nitrogen ceiling moves the dairy yield toward the low-intensity bound by the same pressure the crops face. Yield, milk revenue and reported output move together - the output coefficient is scaled by the extensification, so the margin cannot steer the solve while leaving production unchanged, which is the failure the crop yield shocks had. IDENTITY WHEN SLACK, by construction: no ceiling, no effect. Base fidelity 0.58% and all 8 anchors unchanged. Under a 100 kg N/ha ceiling in NL11 the herd falls 1.6% while milk output falls 10.5% - the herd extensifies as well as shrinking. Pinned by test_livestock_intensity_margin_is_identity_when_unconstrained, which asserts output falls faster than the herd, so an inert margin would fail.

fitness_for_use_declaration.note: Every other file in capri_data records where an INPUT came from. Nothing recorded how far an OUTPUT could be trusted in a form anything could read: the fitness-for-use knowledge - 'oilseed and permanent-crop magnitudes are overstated', 'multi-period herd paths are not meaningful', 'Croatian regional results are not reliable individually' - lived in README prose. A caller holding a number had no programmatic way to learn it was one the authors say not to rely on. That is the reverse of the usual risk: scrupulous about input provenance, silent about output reliability. FITNESS_FOR_USE.json now declares 19 outputs with a status (validated, use_with_care, overstated, understated, not_supported), a note, and where relevant a scope, a reference and a ratio against CAPRI. capri_mod/fitness.py queries it, falling back from the specific key to the general one, so 'scenario.permanent_crops' resolves before 'scenario'. An unrecorded key returns 'unknown' rather than 'validated' - silence is not a clean bill of health. Pinned by test_fitness_for_use_is_consistent_with_the_model, which checks the vocabulary, that every non-validated entry actually yields a caveat, and that every region named in a scope exists. That test caught two flaws in itself while being written: EU27 is a trade region rather than a NUTS-2 region, and 'rice' is four letters. WRITING IT ALSO CAUGHT TWO STALE README CLAIMS in the 'Not sound for' list: farm income was still described as contaminated although it had been fixed, and permanent crops as responding at half CAPRI's figure when they now overshoot at 1.39x.

not_sound_for_items_fixed.status: three of the list fixed; four confirmed unfixable with available data, each for a stated reason
not_sound_for_items_fixed.note: Each item in README section 9's 'Not sound for' list was tested for fixability against the data now held, including the user's conversions of the public JRC CAPRI dataset. FIXED - WINE. The list said 101 regions lacked a CAPRI wine price. Only 11 of those actually grow wine (338 kha); the rest have no vineyards, so the missing price was irrelevant there. For the 11, CAPRI has no regional revenue either, but it does have NATIONAL prices: Italy 1,362, Croatia 1,923, Slovenia 1,858 EUR/t. The loader now falls back regional -> national -> EU, where it used to drop straight to the EU-wide 95.5. Sicily's 127 kha moves from 95.5 to 1,361.6. Zero vine-growing regions remain without a price. National table: capri_data/sources/capreg/capreg_national_prices.csv. FIXED - CROATIA. The split across HR03 (Adriatic) and HR04 (Continental) used one cattle key for every crop, which put 91% of Croatia's olives in continental Croatia. CAPRI's own regional selection (capreg/regio_data_sel/p_REGIO, from the public JRC dataset) holds HR03's per-crop areas; HR04 is the national remainder, which is exact. Olives move HR03 1.8 -> 18.0 kha, wine 2.0 -> 14.2, and wheat 2.2 (it is continental). The olive mapping is VERIFIED rather than assumed: REGIO's OLIT for HR03 in 2013 is 18.6 kha, exactly CAPRI's national Croatian olive area. VINE for wine is CAPRI's own concordance entry. FIXED - SAXONY. CAPRI holds Saxony as one region; the three Direktionsbezirke were split by cattle share. REGIO holds them under the pre-2013 codes (DED1 Chemnitz, DED2 Dresden, DED3 Leipzig), so each crop is now split by its own 2003-2007 shares. Maize: upland Chemnitz 7.1 -> 0.9 kha, lowland Leipzig 2.4 -> 7.8. National totals are preserved to the hectare for both countries (Croatia 1,515.4, Saxony 912.7); herds keep the cattle key, which is the right key for cattle. NOT FIXABLE, each for a stated reason: NORWAY NO05 - REGIO holds no crop areas for the four redrawn Norwegian regions. IRISH NITROGEN - no source here records a physical grass yield: CAPRI's grass price is a dummy and its 'yield' equals revenue, and REGIO has no grass YILD either. OILSEED AND PERMANENT-CROP OVERSHOOT - bounded by the published reference, which merges vegetables with permanent crops. MULTI-PERIOD PROJECTIONS - intermediate years have no external reference to validate against. ECONOMY-WIDE EFFECTS - outside the partial-equilibrium boundary by design, as in CAPRI. A GAP EXPOSED ALONG THE WAY: files under sources/ that the model reads directly - the regional and national price tables, p_REGIO - sit outside MANIFEST.json by convention, so the validator's shape check does not cover them. Worth closing.

eu_armington_price_formation.status: FIXED - the cause of the oilseed and permanent-crop overshoot
eu_armington_price_formation.note: WHY THE LEVELS WERE OVERSTATED. Under Farm-to-Fork the model's EU prices rose +3.0% (cereals), +1.6% (oilseeds) and +2.5% (vegetables and permanent crops) where CAPRI reports +8%, +12% and +15%. The price shortfall was worst exactly where the quantity overshoot was (oilseeds 0.13x CAPRI's price rise, vegetables and permanent crops 0.17x) and mildest where quantities matched (cereals 0.38x). In CAPRI the price rise holds supply up; here it did not, so supply kept falling. TWO STRUCTURAL CAUSES. (1) Every regional price was a fixed wedge on the world price, p_domestic = p_world x (1+tariff). The model HAD Armington parameters, but they only apportioned a region's imports among supplier countries; they never entered price formation. So the EU was a price-taker: an EU supply cut was filled by imports at an unchanged price - the law of one price, not an Armington market. (2) The supply side responded to the WORLD price, not the EU price, so even a correct EU price would never have reached farmers. An earlier diagnosis in this investigation called the substitution elasticities 'GTAP-style'; that was wrong - they are CAPRI's own values (special_ch/market1_ch.gms sets APPL 2.8/5.6 and BARL 3.2/6.4, exactly as held). The parameters were right; they were simply not governing prices. THE FIX. An EU Armington price premium from the standard first-order condition, (p_D/p_D0) = ((M/D)/(M0/D0))^(1/sigma) for a net importer and its mirror on the export share for a net exporter, with CAPRI's sigma and bounds of [0.67, 1.5]. It is solved as a small fixed point inside the market because a higher EU price lowers EU demand. Supply now responds to the EU price (world change x premium). The base is recorded at the model's own levels from a converged baseline run for the same region set, so the premium is exactly 1 at base: all 8 regression anchors are unchanged. A COBWEB FOLLOWED AND WAS FIXED. Price and supply now feed back on each other, and taking each new price signal in full made the outer loop diverge (maximum price change 0.19 -> 0.33). A relaxation of 0.4 on the supply price signal fixes it; it changes the path, not the equilibrium. Convergence now also requires the signal to have reached its target, since damped steps are small by design and could otherwise pass for convergence. RESULT, EU-wide, all 248 regions, converged in 11 outer iterations (market converged too): oilseeds -13.9% against CAPRI's -15% (0.93, was 1.40), price +9.5% against +12%; vegetables and permanent crops -12.6% against -12% (1.05, was 1.39), price +8.8% against +15%; cereals -9.8% against -15% (0.65, was 0.93), price +7.5% against +8%. WHAT CEREALS REVEAL. The cereal PRICE is now almost exactly CAPRI's, but the QUANTITY falls less. So the earlier near-perfect cereal match was partly two errors cancelling: a price far too low had offset some other shortfall. That remaining cereal gap is now exposed and is the next question. ALSO FIXED: paddy rice was missing from the supply-to-market bridge, so the model's own rice production never reached the rice market. COST: runs now take more outer iterations (11 here), so a converged EU-wide comparison is slower. Pinned by test_eu_armington_premium_is_inert_at_base_and_responds_to_supply.

arable_land_conservation.status: FIXED - the cause of the cereal-quantity shortfall
arable_land_conservation.note: The arable land constraint left out set-aside (SETA) and fodder on arable land (MAIF, OFOD). Consequences: (1) a landscape-feature floor on SETA grew set-aside out of nothing - in DE40 set-aside rose 52 kha, cereals were unchanged and total area rose 52 kha; land was not conserved. In CAPRI fallow competes for arable land, which is where its -9% cereal-area effect under Farm-to-Fork comes from. (2) The right-hand side counted fodder land while the sum did not, leaving ~14 Mha of built-in slack, so the row could never bind: the arable shadow price was zero in every region - a finding recorded early in this project and misread as 'land is not the binding channel'. Also: tobacco, cotton and other fibre sat in the PERMANENT row while the land data counts them as arable (they are annuals). Both rows now use one classification, PERMANENT_LAND_CROPS, the same set tools/build/build_capri_base.py builds the land data with. Arable availability now includes fallow. RESULT: base fidelity IMPROVED 0.59% -> 0.22%; all 8 anchors hold. Farm-to-Fork cereal production 0.65x -> 0.96x CAPRI. Land is conserved: in DE40 a 10% floor now takes 5.4% of the cereal area.

capri_greendeal_targets_ms.note: CAPRI's own per-member-state Green Deal targets, from gams/pol_input/greendeal/landscape_targets.gdx, organic_targets.gdx and organic_targets_uaa.gdx (dumped by the project lead with gdxdump; raw dumps in sources/capri_gams/greendeal/). Stored as 2017/policy/landscape_targets_ms.csv and organic_targets_ms.csv. LANDSCAPE: implemented as CAPRI's landscape.gms rule, FALL.FLOOR = lndscpTarg/10 * p_setAsideTarget * UAAR + SETF, where p_setAsideTarget is the member state's MISSING share net of fallow and of LUCAS landscape elements; a member state with no entry (CY, ES, FI) is already at the target. An earlier hypothesis here was that CAPRI demands LESS new land than a flat 10%; the data shows the opposite - 10,276 kha against 9,641 - so the EU total was about right and the distribution was what differed. ORGANIC: CAPRI does not move each member state to 25%. Its per-MS values weight to exactly 15.0 points EU-wide, i.e. they burden-share the 15-point shock (25% target minus 10% existing), and they differ by crop group: France converts 45.6% of permanent crops and 19.8% of arable land; Austria, already past 25%, still converts 7.5 points of UAA where the earlier distance-to-25% rule gave it nothing. Conversion is now per member state and crop group (arable, permanent grassland, permanent crops), falling back to the UAA-wide figure. The requested share scales the ambition (0.25 = CAPRI's target). RESULT, EU-wide, converged: cereals -15.3% against CAPRI's -15% (1.02); oilseeds -19.8% against -15% (1.32); vegetables and permanent crops -14.1% against -12% (1.18).

eu_market_base_balance.note: Diagnosing why EU prices now rise further than CAPRI's (cereals +14.4% against +8%) showed the market's EU27 BASE balance is inconsistent with FAO: base consumption of wheat 28.5 Mt against a real 108.9, of maize 194.8 Mt against 80.4; base rapeseed production 6.6 Mt against 16.9. The market therefore sees the EU as a 76 Mt wheat exporter (really ~30). The Armington premium is computed on these ratios, and the world price also rises (+4-7% for cereals) as EU exports fall; the two together overshoot. The premium formula is NOT the fault and was deliberately not tuned to hit CAPRI's price figures - doing so on wrong balances would be two errors cancelling. The fix is to calibrate EU demand in the market to FAO consumption. It affects every market result, not only Farm-to-Fork. Also recorded: FAO's EU27 import and export figures include intra-EU trade (wheat imports 45.9 Mt), so they are not the bloc's gross trade and must not be used as such; the net position is valid because intra-EU flows cancel.
eu_market_base_balance.root_cause: ROOT CAUSE FOUND - a design decision, not a data problem. The market derives each region's base consumption as production minus net exports. Net exports come from shared/trade_flows_2017.csv and are RIGHT for the EU: intra-EU trade sits on the EU27->EU27 diagonal and is correctly excluded, leaving extra-EU wheat net exports of +27.9 Mt (real ~25-30). The error is EU PRODUCTION. EU27 is deliberately excluded from the real-FAO production override (the comment: its supply comes from the supply module at solve time, and injecting FAO levels would 'unbalance the base'). Excluded, it becomes a residual of a hard-coded world total (world_prod_ref) minus every region that does have real data: wheat 55.9 Mt against a real ~139, maize 169.0 against ~73, rapeseed 2.7 against ~17. Consumption inherits the error (wheat 55.9 - 27.9 = 28.1 Mt). A single world demand-calibration factor then rescales every region's demand, spreading the inconsistency worldwide. THE DATA NEEDED IS ALREADY HELD: fao_market_baseline.json carries correct EU27 production and consumption (wheat 138.7 and 108.9 Mt). PROPOSED FIX: take EU base consumption from FAO; take EU base production from the supply module's own base output, so the premium and the solve see one consistent EU; close the world balance through the residual region (ROW) instead of rescaling every region's demand. Expect the base-year market to move, so price reproduction (12/12) and world imbalance must be re-checked. ON INTRA-EU TRADE: no extra data is needed. FAO's EU27 import and export totals include intra-EU trade and must not be used as the bloc's trade, but the model does not need them - the trade flow file already separates intra-EU flows. Gross extra-EU trade would only be needed for a gross-flow Armington, and would then come from Eurostat Comext (extra-EU) or CAPRI's own market results.
eu_market_base_balance.fix: EU production in the market is now the supply module's own base output and EU consumption keeps FAO's EU consumption-to-production ratio (one source, one set of definitions, so the EU's real self-sufficiency even where levels differ); the world balance closes over the other regions. EU base consumption: wheat 99.4 Mt (was 28.4), maize 72.7 (was 194); implied net trade consistent with reality. The baseline now converges in 2 outer iterations instead of 11, because it starts in equilibrium.

scenario_convergence_and_speed.note: With a correct EU balance the Armington premium finally bit, and Farm-to-Fork stopped converging. Found by a live per-iteration trace naming the moving commodities. Four changes: (1) GROSS-TRADE premium: a two-sided Armington clearing (production = domestic sales + exports; domestic sales compete with imports at sigma, exports compete abroad at rho2) replaces a net-trade ratio that moved several-fold where net positions were small. Gross trade enters as a scale-free two-way intensity from the trade file, which separates intra-EU flows correctly, rebuilt around the market's own net position so the base closes exactly; levels could not be used (rapeseed imports 28.6 Mt against a consumption of 10.1). (2) PREMIUM ONLY FOR TRADED GOODS (recorded gross trade >= 5% of EU consumption): sugar beet, with no recorded trade, flipped between the premium bounds every iteration (1.500 -> 0.744 -> 1.500) and alone kept the loop from settling. (3) THE MARKET ANTICIPATES THE SUPPLY RESPONSE with CAPRI's own market-level supply elasticities, as CAPRI's market module does, so the 248 regional supply models only correct an approximation; this changes the path, not the equilibrium. (4) Relaxation 0.5: at 0.7 the loop fell into a clean two-state cycle. RESULT: Farm-to-Fork converges in 6 iterations; a full comparison takes ~10 min (18.5 before, 8 on this morning's wrong-balance code). Cereals -15.0% against CAPRI's -15% (1.00); oilseeds -22.2% against -15% (1.48) with the price ABOVE CAPRI's, so the oilseed overshoot is on the supply side; vegetables and permanent crops -14.6% against -12% (1.21). Prices: cereals +15.6% against +8%, oilseeds +15.7% against +12%, vegetables and permanent crops +6.7% against +15%. DATA GAP: the trade file records no trade for sugar and durum wheat, both of which are traded; their EU prices follow the world price with no premium, and durum's world price rises 10% under Farm-to-Fork partly for that reason.

run_history_dependence.note: Results depended on what a model instance had done before. (1) A run with a world price shock overwrote the market's base world prices and nothing restored them, so every later run inherited the shock - a baseline after a +20% wheat-price run gave DE11 wheat 111.2 instead of 91.2. OLDER than the current work; exposed by it. (2) The market calibration froze at the first solve an instance ever performed. Both fixed: each run starts from the true base prices, each baseline recalibrates, and scenario runs reuse the calibration of the baseline for the same region set. Caught by test_projection_null_trajectory_reproduces_base, which now passes even after a deliberately price-shocked first run on a region subset.

oilseed_area_overshoot_pesticide_channel.status: PARTLY FIXED - CAPRI conventional-area rule implemented; oilseed asymmetry remains
oilseed_area_overshoot_pesticide_channel.note: DECOMPOSITION (Farm-to-Fork, converged): oilseed yields fall ~10% (rapeseed -10.0, sunflower -10.1), close to CAPRI's -11% for cereals, so the yield channel is right; the excess is AREA - rapeseed -12.2%, sunflower -13.1%, soybeans -28.7% - against the ~5% implied by CAPRI's -15% oilseed figure. INSTRUMENT BY INSTRUMENT (each alone, EU-wide): landscape floor oilseeds -10.4% / cereals -8.8% (CAPRI's report attributes -9% of cereal area to landscape elements, so this channel MATCHES); pesticides oilseeds -4.2% / cereals +0.9%; organic -0.5% / +0.6%; nutrients -0.2% / -0.4%. The asymmetry is the pesticide channel: halving plant-protection spending while raising other inputs 50% makes wheat cheaper to grow (-4.1% of cost; PPP share 17.6%) and rapeseed dearer (+4.4%; PPP share 6.6%). CAPRI'S RULE, NOT FOLLOWED HERE (pol_input/greendeal/pesticides.gms -> conventional_io.gms): the 50% pesticide cut is a TOTAL target. Organic conversion already delivers part of it; the REMAINING cut, max(0, 50% - organic share) / (1 - organic share), is applied to the CONVENTIONAL area only, so the overall reduction stays 50%. This model applies the full 50% cut, the 10% yield loss and the +50% other costs to every hectare, including those organic conversion already took to zero plant protection - a double count wherever the two instruments combine, largest where organic conversion is high. FIX: scale the pesticide changes per activity by the conventional share, with the plant-protection cut set to the remaining target. Expected to shrink the pesticide channel; whether it removes the oilseed asymmetry is open, since that also reflects rapeseed's low plant-protection share - which comes from CAPRI's own cost data. Also noted: CAPRI's report gives EU cereal imports +39% and exports -38% under Farm-to-Fork, a trade-side check not yet made.
oilseed_area_overshoot_pesticide_channel.fix: IMPLEMENTED: per crop with organic share o, the plant-protection cut is the remaining target max(0, 50% - o) and the 10% yield loss and +50% other inputs fall on the conventional share (1 - o) only; with no organic instrument nothing changes. Pinned by test_pesticide_target_applies_to_conventional_area_only. RESULT (Farm-to-Fork, converged in 6): vegetables and permanent crops 1.21x -> 1.08x (-12.9% against -12%) - where organic conversion is highest, so the double count was largest; oilseeds 1.48x -> 1.40x (-21.0% against -15%); cereals 1.00x -> 0.95x (-14.3%). Prices: cereals +14.7%, oilseeds +14.6%, vegetables and permanent crops +5.8% against CAPRI's +8/+12/+15. Oilseed AREA barely moved (rapeseed -12.2% -> -11.8%): the remaining asymmetry comes from the pesticide cost channel acting on rapeseed's low plant-protection share (6.6%, from CAPRI's own cost data), and needs CAPRI's per-crop Farm-to-Fork results to localise further.

oilseed_seed_quantity_bridge.note: The supply-to-market bridge multiplied rapeseed and sunflower SEED production by the OIL extraction yield (0.42) and passed the result to the SEED commodities, which carry seed world prices and whose EU demand is calibrated to FAO seed use, crushing included. The market saw EU rapeseed at 7.4 Mt and sunflower at 4.1, against ~19 and ~10 produced by the supply side and 22.4 and 10.7 in CAPRI's own 2030 reference. Percentage changes survived the constant factor, which is why it went unnoticed; the EU's weight in the world oilseed markets did not, so world prices under-reacted to EU oilseed supply. FOUND by comparing against CAPRI's EU27 market balance from res_2_1730greendeal_refdefaulta.gdx, which the project lead had already supplied as gd_full.txt - only activity levels had ever been read from it. Stored as capri_data/validation/capri_eu27_market_balance_2030_ref.json. The same comparison CONFIRMS the corrected EU market balance: EU self-sufficiency wheat 1.27 (CAPRI 2030 1.31), maize 0.91 (0.93), rapeseed 0.73 (0.76). RESULT (Farm-to-Fork, converged in 6): oilseeds 1.40x -> 1.33x (-20.0% against -15%), rapeseed area -11.8% -> -10.7%; cereals 0.96x, vegetables and permanent crops 1.08x unchanged.

capri_mitigation_technologies.note: CAPRI's own mitigation technology data (dat/scen/ghgtech p_ghgMiti, from the public JRC dataset) stored as 2017/abatement/capri_ghg_mitigation.csv: 27 member states, 20 options, 1,296 option-activity-country combinations. ADOPTION RULE from CAPRI's objective (supply/supply_model.gms, GHG_Mit_Cost_): cost per unit of activity (costParLin - revenue + pmpParLin - subsidy)*s + 0.5*(costParSqr + pmpParSqr)*s^2, so the optimal share is s* = (price x saving - a)/b within [0, MaxShare]; savings are relative to CAPRI's no-change technology (Q_tech/Q_noc), so CAPRI's absolute units never enter. Implemented in capri_mod/abatement/capri_mitigation.py (not yet wired into the model). VERIFIED: at a zero carbon price the rule reproduces CAPRI's calibrated initial share for all 245 options that have one, and gives zero for all 1,051 that do not - confirming the cost function, signs and calibration terms. VALIDATION AGAINST CAPRI'S MAXIMUM-POTENTIAL RUN (res_2_1730greendeal_refpol_endotech_all_max, supplied by the project lead; ghgTechCali=max): EU27 emissions against the 2030 reference - enteric CH4 -24.9%, manure CH4 -33.2%, rice CH4 -14.6%, synthetic-fertiliser N2O -28.9%, agricultural GWP -25.1%; herds change only +1-4%, so the reductions are technology. The 20 table options reach only enteric -3.7% and manure -11.3% at maximum adoption. CAUSE: the max run also switches on option families defined in CAPRI's GAMS code, not in the technology table - linseed and nitrate feed additives (ghgTechLineNitr), low-protein feeding (ghgTechLowNFeed), a 10% feed-efficiency gain (ghgTechFEff), winter cover and fallow, secondary fertilisers, endogenous ammonia measures. The miti_data_jul15 table the run reads has FEWER options (9), not more. Also: alternative rice options were stacked multiplicatively in the first comparison (-72%); they are mutually exclusive shares and must not be stacked. NEXT: add the code-defined option families (envind/linenitr.gms, low_n_feed.gms, breeding.gms, no_histosols.gms) with their data, treat options competing for the same activity and gas as shares summing to at most one, wire into the model, and re-compare against the max run.
capri_mitigation_technologies.correction: CORRECTION to the figures above. CAPRI's AGGT values are PER UNIT of an aggregate activity level, and in the max run that aggregate grows 17.1% (it counts the winter-cover and fallow activities the mitigation options create). The per-unit changes first quoted here (-24.9% enteric, -33.2% manure CH4, -14.6% rice, -28.9% N2OSYN, -25.1% GWPA) therefore overstated the reductions. As TOTALS (item x AGGT level), max vs reference: enteric CH4 -12.0%, manure CH4 -21.8%, rice CH4 0.0%, N2OSYN -16.7%, N2OMAN -30.0%, N2OHIS -97.6%, GWPA -12.3%; the ini run is at the reference (GWPA -0.3%). Confirmed bottom-up: per-head CH4ENT times herd over the 17 elementary livestock activities gives -11.9% (-13.7% at unchanged herds). The gap to the 20 table options (enteric -3.7%, manure -11.3% at maximum) is real but about half what was first stated. ALSO FOUND: CAPRI records the adoption it reached (qualifier SHARE, with MaxShare, cost, pmpcost, revenue) per country, activity and option; EU dairy in the max run: nitrate alone 0.39, linseed+nitrate (AComLN) 0.24, low-protein feeding 0.59, anaerobic digestion 0.20, plus ammonia measures (low-emission housing, covered storage, low-emission application) this model does not represent. CAPRI's additive reductions (envind/line_nitr.gms): linseed 5% per 1% DM fat up to 5% (-25%), nitrate 10% per 1% DM up to 1.5% (-15%; replacement heifers 1% -> -10%), combined multiplicatively (-36%), 3-NOP ~-32% with diet adjustments; each limited to stabled animals.
capri_mitigation_technologies.mechanics_and_data: MECHANICS TESTED: per animal category, CAPRI's realised additive shares combined with its own additive formulas explain about 70-80% of the per-head enteric CH4 cut in the max run (dairy DCOH -14.7% of -18.1%, DCOL -16.1% of -21.7%, suckler cows -4.9% of -7.5%); the systematic remainder is consistent with diet effects, since CAPRI computes enteric CH4 from feed intake and the max run also changes diets (low-protein feeding, feed-efficiency gain). DATA STORED: capri_data/validation/capri_mitigation_shares_2030.csv - CAPRI's maximum and realised adoption shares for every member state, activity and option in both runs (16,736 rows, 33 options). In the max run most options sit exactly at their maximum (DE dairy: anaerobic digestion 0.471/0.471, nitrate 0.779/0.779, low-protein feeding 0.313/0.313), so it is CAPRI's full technical potential - the benchmark for the upper end of a MACC. EU27 extracts of both runs: capri_data/validation/capri_eu27_refpol_endotech_{ini,max}_2030.txt.
capri_mitigation_technologies.implementation: capri_mod/abatement/capri_mitigation.py, class CapriAbatement, wired into CAPRIModel.run (results 'abatement_capri', with run_abatement=True; carbon_price sets the price). HOW FAR: per member state and source, the share of emissions CAPRI removes at full technical potential (max run against its 2030 reference, at reference herds) - 2017/abatement/capri_mitigation_potential.csv; it covers CAPRI's whole portfolio incl. feed additives, diet and ammonia measures. Soil N2O uses an EU-level 5.6% (fertiliser N2O -16.7% at about a third of soil N2O), because CAPRI's country-level aggregates grow 1.5-3.7x in the max run and are not usable as totals. HOW FAR AT A PRICE: CAPRI's own adoption rule on the options with published cost functions, as a fraction of their potential beyond the initial adoption already in the reference; ASSUMPTION: code-defined options follow the same price response per gas. RESULTS on this model's own emissions, EU-wide: full potential enteric -10.8% (CAPRI -12.0%), manure CH4 -22.3% (-21.8%), manure N2O -29.4% (-30.0%); total 18.3% of agricultural GHG against CAPRI's -12.3% GWPA, the gap being inventory composition (CAPRI's total includes categories no option touches). Price curve, share of agricultural GHG: 0% at 0 EUR/t, then rising monotonically. A first version counted CAPRI's initial adoption as abatement at zero price (0.46%); fixed. Pinned by test_capri_mitigation_reproduces_capri.
capri_mitigation_technologies.valuation_fix: FIXED BEFORE RELEASE: the price response first valued every option with one crude EU-wide emission per unit, and two of those were mis-scaled (manure CH4 per head divided by the wrong total; fertiliser N2O ~1000x too small), so manure options barely responded and soil options never did. Each option is now valued with its own country's baseline: CAPRI's no-change QEmitt is kg CH4 per head per year (dairy enteric 70.6 x 25 = 1.76 t CO2e, against this model's 1.68); for fertiliser N2O, whose unit the data does not give, a documented 0.47 t CO2e/ha. Share of potential adopted: 10 EUR/t enteric 0.09 / manure 0.11 / soil 0.00; 50 EUR/t 0.66 / 0.42 / 0.00; 100 EUR/t 0.83 / 0.66 / 0.03; 200 EUR/t 0.99 / 0.88 / 0.21.

farm_to_fork_trade_check.status: passed, with the durum data gap visible
farm_to_fork_trade_check.note: CAPRI's report (JRC121368) gives EU cereal imports +39% and exports -38% under Farm-to-Fork. This model's gross flows, rebuilt by market_module.eu_gross_trade from the same Armington clearing it solves with (nothing tuned to these numbers): imports +49.5%, exports -44.1%, converged. Excluding durum wheat, which has no recorded trade and so starts from zero imports, cereal imports rise +40.1% - against CAPRI's +39%. Wheat: imports 6.4 -> 8.4 Mt, exports 33.5 -> 18.1 Mt; barley exports 14.2 -> 8.6 Mt; maize imports 6.6 -> 9.8 Mt. The remaining export excess (-44% against -38%) is consistent with cereal prices rising more than CAPRI's (+14.8% against +8%).

durum_sugar_trade_supplement.status: sugar fixed; durum remains a gap, for a stated reason
durum_sugar_trade_supplement.note: The trade file records no trade for sugar and durum wheat, so neither could carry an Armington premium. CAPRI's own 2030 reference supplies extra-EU trade: imports from the NONEU partner aggregate (= World minus intra-EU), exports = imports + net exports (EXPT - IMPT; intra-EU flows cancel). Sugar: imports 2,969 kt, exports 855 kt. CAPRI's market trades wheat as ONE commodity (WHEA), so durum can only be proxied from wheat's pattern (WHEA imports 3,171, exports 34,185 kt) scaled by durum's share of wheat production. Stored as 2017/market/eu_gross_trade_supplement.csv, used only where the trade file records nothing. ARCHIVED 20 October 2026 (capri_data/archive/): only the premium market structure used it, removed with that structure (KNOWN_ISSUES K54-2); the bilateral market reads CAPRI's bilateral flows. FIRST ATTEMPT BROKE CONVERGENCE: durum passed the recorded-trade test, but the market sees the EU durum balance as almost exactly even, so the rebuilt flows fell to the 91 kt floor and the premium turned so steep that Farm-to-Fork hit the 15-iteration cap. FIX: the traded-goods rule now applies to the REBUILT flows the premium uses, in both the premium and the eu_gross_trade report; durum sits out again, sugar keeps its trade, and Farm-to-Fork converges in 7. THE DURUM GAP IS THE BALANCE, NOT THE TRADE: the EU is a real net importer of durum, but the market's EU durum balance is near-even; fixing it needs durum-specific production and use, which CAPRI's market does not separate.
